rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 (Figures 4-1, 5-1 to 5-7) report the authors' own Proteus simulation runs of a Raspberry Pi/MCP3208 sensor framework with simulated temperature, pressure, soil moisture and rain-detection data over a one-hour period, plus a mobile app and ThingSpeak integration.
rows.notes: The study is a design-and-simulation paper, not a field trial. It reports simulated sensor outputs generated from predefined ranges (temperature 20-40 C, pressure 1010-1025 hPa, soil moisture 10-50%) and shows that alerts and a moving-average forecast can be displayed in a mobile app. No crop was grown, no yield, water use or environmental outcome was measured, and the simulation was never compared with measurements from a real system (Section 5.5 and Section 6 explicitly state it used predefined data and no real-world devices). The paper only asserts, citing other work [18],[19], that such monitoring 'ensures efficient irrigation' and 'increases yields'. It therefore offers no own evidence on the claimed effect of IoT soil sensors on crop yields or environmental impact; at most it demonstrates a monitoring/alerting precondition. Q8 is 'no' because the stated limitations (predefined data, no calibration, experimental setup) concern the simulation itself, not any result on the yield claim, which the study does not report.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Figures are not reproduced but their content is described in the text. The paper's results are entirely from a Proteus circuit simulation with synthetic input data; no field deployment, crop or yield data exist in the study.
